source_text: Cum in primo volumine perspicuis definitionibus constitisset Deum ita iustum esse, ut, si probari posset iustus non esse, convinceretur Deus non esse, cumque super hoc remansisset nulla dubitatio, claruit etiam iustitiam nihil esse aliud quam virtutem numquam quidquam inique iudicantem, nihil inique facientem, sed reddentem sua unicuique sine fraude sine gratia, id est sine personarum acceptione.
pass_a_gloss: When in the first volume it had stood by clear definitions that God is just in such a way that, if it could be proved he was not just, he would be convicted not to be God, and when no doubt had remained over this, it also became clear that justice is nothing other than the virtue never judging anything unfairly, doing nothing unfairly, but rendering to each his own without fraud, without favor—that is, without acceptance of persons.

lemmas.lexica: LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: In the first book, clear definitions established that God is just in such a way that, if he could be proved unjust, he would be proved not to be God. Once no doubt remained about this, it also became clear that justice is simply the virtue that never judges unfairly or acts unfairly, but gives each person what belongs to that person, without deception or favoritism—that is, without showing partiality (Romans 2:11).

choices.why: In the suum cuique definition gratia is partiality, not saving grace.
Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: The explanation without partiality may echo Paul’s formula concerning God’s impartiality.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
